headline: Parliament Passes Auckland Housing Bill Cutting Minimum Capacity to 1.4 Million
summary: Parliament passed an urgent Auckland housing amendment that lowers the city’s minimum planned housing capacity from about 2 million homes to 1.4 million, prompting a sharp dispute over affordability, infrastructure and who will carry the burden of growth. Ministers said the change gives Auckland Council more flexibility to plan around transport and local constraints; opponents argued it could reduce housing opportunities and was rushed through without enough scrutiny. MPs also debated fuel security and cost-of-living support, advanced a contested fisheries bill to select committee, and completed committee consideration of legislation to close greyhound racing.

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Housing Minimum Cut to 1.4 Million in Urgent Bill
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill changes the minimum housing capacity Auckland must plan for, affecting future housing supply, affordability and where growth may occur.
topicSummaries.content: The Resource Management (Auckland Housing) Amendment Bill passed its third reading by 68 votes to 55 after being introduced and advanced through all stages under urgency. It reduces the minimum housing capacity requirement by 32.5 percent, from a figure of about 2 million to approximately 1.4 million, while leaving requirements for intensification around specified rapid-transit stations and centres in place. Housing Minister Chris Bishop and Associate Minister Tama Potaka said the change allows Auckland Council to better account for infrastructure, flood risk and community input; Bishop said existing Plan Change 120 submissions remain valid and people can update them as revised maps are produced. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bill, arguing that the lower minimum could constrain housing supply, leave West and South Auckland carrying more growth, and weaken public and mana whenua participation. The Government said the council can still plan for more than 1.4 million homes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Penny Simmonds (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is about smarter growth, not slower growth—growth that is better aligned with infrastructure, with transport, and with employment patterns.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: because make no mistake: this bill will result in less housing opportunities and fewer houses for Aucklanders.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Weighs Fuel Guarantees as Stocks Are Monitored
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Fuel supply and any public guarantees for importers could affect transport, businesses and the public finances during a period of international supply uncertainty.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis reported that New Zealand had about 59 days of petrol, 54 days of diesel and 50 days of jet fuel in the country, its exclusive economic zone or on ships heading here. She said two technical triggers in the fuel response plan had been met, but the latest data showed no material deterioration in supply risk, so the Government would not begin a formal phase assessment. Cabinet is exploring additional supply options, including converting international energy agency fuel options into usable stocks and potentially offering indemnities, guarantees or loans to support commercial fuel purchases, subject to safeguards for public finances. Opposition Leader Chris Hipkins challenged the Government over cancelling a planned strategic diesel reserve and delaying higher stockholding requirements; Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defended reliance on fuel companies’ obligations.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Did his Government’s cancelling of the planned 70 million litre strategic diesel reserve increase or decrease New Zealand’s exposure to a diesel supply shock?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, what this Government did is it cancelled Labour’s approach by putting fuel companies on the hook to making sure that they meet their obligations to hold higher levels of stocks.

keyExchanges.speaker: Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Government under any phase of the National Fuel Plan offer a financial underwrite or guarantee to fuel companies, as Australia is doing?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Cabinet has agreed in principle that indemnities, guarantees, or loans to support commercial arrangements may be necessary in the public interest

topicSummaries.topic: Fuel Relief Targets 143,000 Working Families as Benefits Rise
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The eligibility rules determine which households receive extra help with fuel and other essential costs as prices rise.
topicSummaries.content: The Government said a $50-a-week increase in the in-work tax credit would go to about 143,000 families with children and paid employment from 1 April. Separately, annual adjustments will raise financial support for more than 1.5 million people, including beneficiaries, superannuitants, students and some people receiving supplementary assistance. Labour questioned why the targeted fuel payment did not include some solo parents, grandparents raising children and parents of disabled children who work part-time while receiving assistance. Social Development Minister Louise Upston said main-benefit recipients are not eligible for the in-work tax credit but would receive annual payment increases, and defended targeted assistance over broader spending on inflation grounds. Penny Simmonds also corrected an earlier answer, clarifying that not all children in material hardship live in households eligible for the in-work tax credit.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willow-Jean Prime (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why didn’t the Government’s response target solo parents who are raising children and working part-time while receiving part of a benefit?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our Government’s been clear about the support that is available for New Zealanders.

topicSummaries.topic: Fisheries Amendment Bill Passes First Reading Amid Sustainability Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Proposed changes to commercial fishing rules could affect fish stocks, recreational and customary fishing, and livelihoods across the seafood sector.
topicSummaries.content: The Fisheries Amendment Bill passed its first reading by 68 votes to 55 and was referred to the Primary Production Committee, with a report due by 6 August. Oceans and Fisheries Minister Shane Jones said the bill aims to improve commercial efficiency and manage litigation, including by setting a 20-working-day limit for judicial reviews, recognising some industry-led measures and changing deemed-value settings. The proposal would also restrict access to commercial fishing camera footage. Opposition speakers raised concerns about transparency, self-reporting, environmental protections and consultation with recreational, customary and Māori commercial fishers. National supported the first reading but said it could oppose the bill at its next stage if it is not significantly improved. The Government said the proposal for commercial fishers to retain undersized fish would be removed during the select committee process after public objections.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shane Jones (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: The bill introduces a 20-working-day limit for lodging judicial reviews of decisions under the Act.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: However, the Labour Party will not be supporting this bill this afternoon, and that’s because it actually is a retrograde step backwards in terms of the role that New Zealand has all around the world when it comes to fishing.

keyExchanges.speaker: Grant McCallum (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Ultimately, if National is not happy with the bill following the select committee process, we will not support it at second reading.

topicSummaries.topic: Greyhound Racing Closure Bill Advances Without Compensation Amendments
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The closure will end an industry and affect animal rehoming, workers’ livelihoods and the transition support available to participants.
topicSummaries.content: The House completed committee consideration of the Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Bill and reported it without amendment; further stages remained. Racing Minister Winston Peters cited investigations dating to 2013, 2017 and 2021 and argued that the industry had been warned about animal-welfare concerns. He said a transition agency would oversee rehoming and could provide support, including for lost income where considered necessary. ACT MP Cameron Luxton sought an independent review of financial losses and a compensation scheme, while Green MP Steve Abel proposed narrowing the review to retraining support. The amendments were rejected. Peters said the transition is estimated to cost $60 million over three years, with most funding expected from TAB overseas greyhound racing revenue and industry assets; he maintained that full compensation was not warranted.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Luxton (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: We will say that there must be an arrangement for an independent review of this Act, for the purposes of assessing the extent of the financial loss to any affected person that has resulted from the commencement of this bill.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: The bill allows for support, and the transition agency has flexibility to provide for additional compensation, such as for lost income, should this be seen as necessary.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Finance Amendment Bill Passes Final Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The legislation changes how the Government reports fiscal risks, tax expenditures and longer-term forecasts.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Finance Amendment Bill passed its third reading by 68 votes to 54, with National, ACT and New Zealand First supporting it and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposing it. National MP Ryan Hamilton said it introduces more specific disclosure requirements for fiscal risks, requires publication of a tax expenditure statement and extends the forecasting period to align with current practice. It also repeals the requirement to articulate wellbeing objectives in fiscal documents.

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Transport Governance Bill Committee Debate Continues
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes would shift local transport decisions towards elected Auckland representatives and reshape how long-term transport plans are agreed.
topicSummaries.content: Under urgency, MPs began committee consideration of the Local Government (Auckland Council) (Transport Governance) Amendment Bill, but the House reported progress and the bill was not completed. Associate Transport Minister James Meager said the bill would establish a joint Auckland Regional Transport Committee, transfer most local transport functions from Auckland Transport to Auckland Council, and refocus Auckland Transport as a public-transport services organisation. It would also give local boards specified transport responsibilities and provide for a transition period. Labour raised questions about accessible formats for the proposed 30-year plan and the balance between local-board powers and regional coordination. The Government ended urgency after the first part of the committee debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The aims of this bill are, therefore, simple: to increase democratic accountability and to strengthen long-term transport planning between Auckland Council and the Crown.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tracey McLellan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: there were not the normal opportunities to, essentially, consult with the public.

conclusion: The Government secured passage of its lower Auckland housing-capacity requirement, but disputes over affordability, infrastructure, consultation and the distribution of growth remain unresolved.
